5:3.text: The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken.

provenance.other: “green olive tree” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 52:8 and Jeremiah 11:16. Only Jeremiah 11:16 makes the olive tree a name for the covenant people, and only there are its branches broken and fire kindled upon it.
provenance.significance: Romans 11 supplies the mechanics of Jacob 5 — the wild stock, the grafting, the natural branches — but not the identification of Israel with an olive tree that the Lord himself planted and named. That is Jeremiah's, and Jeremiah's olive tree ends exactly where the middle of this allegory ends: branches broken, fire kindled on it. Jeremiah 11 is a covenant-lawsuit chapter, which is the genre Jacob 5 is working in from 5:41 onward.

5:3.note: 'I will liken thee, O House of Israel, like unto a tame olive tree, which a man took and nourished in his vineyard.' The KJV has only two horticultural systems for this figure and Jacob 5 uses both: an olive tree standing for Israel (Jeremiah 11:16, Hosea 14:6) and a vineyard standing for Israel (Isaiah 5:7). Zenos's first sentence fuses them by planting the olive tree inside the vineyard, which no biblical verse does. Held at moderate because no clause is reproduced; the case is the identification plus the fate of the branches.

5:3.text: In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.

provenance.other: “decayeth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and “waxeth old” in exactly two; Hebrews 8:13 is the only verse in the Bible that holds both, and it is the only place the KJV pairs decay with growing old.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing does theological work the allegory never states. What 'decayeth and waxeth old' in Hebrews 8:13 is the first covenant, made old by the announcement of a new one and 'ready to vanish away' — and what waxes old and begins to decay in Jacob 5:3 is the house of Israel under exactly that covenant. The whole apparatus of the allegory (pruning, grafting, a last nourishing) is then an answer to Hebrews' verdict: the old tree is not allowed to vanish away, it is dug about.

5:3.note: 'And it grew, and waxed old, and began to decay.' Two uncommon KJV words in six, and the one verse that joins them is Hebrews 8:13. The 1830 reading is 'waxed old, and began to decay', preserving the KJV's verb pair intact. Held at moderate rather than high because the collocation is natural English as well as scriptural English, and a writer describing an old tree might reach it unaided; the rarity count is what makes it worth recording.

5:4.text: And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it:

provenance.other: “dig about it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “dung it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Luke 13:8. The verb 'to dig about' a tree exists nowhere else in the Authorized Version, and 'dung' as a transitive verb exists nowhere else either.
provenance.significance: Two of this chapter's most repeated actions are drawn from a single KJV verse in which a servant asks for one more season before a fruitless tree is cut down. That request is also the shape of Jacob 5:27 and 5:50 — 'nourish it a little longer', 'Spare it a little longer' — so the allegory has taken not only the vinedresser's vocabulary but his rhetorical role. What Luke gives in four verses, Zenos runs for seventy-seven.

5:4.note: 'I will prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it.' The pairing recurs across the chapter and reaches its full form at 5:47 ('I have nourished it, and I have digged it, and I have pruned it, and I have dunged it') and 5:76 ('pruned it, and dug about it, and dunged it'), which is Luke 13:8's two verbs together. Neither word is available anywhere else in the KJV, so the phrasing of the Lord of the vineyard's programme of care is Luke's, in a chapter whose subject Luke's parable shares.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24), the cross-reference standing at the head of the allegory

5:7.text: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

provenance.other: “wild olive tree” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:17, and “natural branches” in exactly two, Romans 11:21 and 11:24. Outside Romans 11 the Bible contains no grafting of any kind. But note the orthography: the KJV spells the verb 'graff' at all four places in Romans 11, and Jacob 5 spells it 'graft' throughout, in 1830 as in the current text.
provenance.significance: This is the verse where the claim already entered at 1 Nephi 10:12 and 15:13 is tested at length. There the catalogue argued that Romans 11 is the Book of Mormon's master allegory and named Jacob 5 in advance as the allegory expanded into a parable; here every one of Paul's terms is present and moving — branches broken off, a wild olive tree plucked and grafted in their stead, natural branches preserved elsewhere, and at 5:52-68 the natural branches grafted back into their own tree. Paul's whole point in Romans 11 is that the last of those is coming; Jacob 5 is that clause dramatised. The one thing the Book of Mormon adds to Paul is the nethermost part of the vineyard — the branches hidden elsewhere — which is what the allegory needs in order to be about a New World remnant as well as about Israel.

5:7.note: 'Go and pluck the branches from a wild olive tree, and bring them hither unto me; and we will pluck off those main branches which are beginning to wither away.' Romans 11:17 in reverse order, with Romans 11:19's 'the branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in' behind it. The chapter never quotes Paul continuously, which is why this is an allusion and not a quotation; what it does instead is run his figure forward for seventy-seven verses. The 'graff'/'graft' spelling difference is worth registering as a limit on how mechanical the borrowing is: the concept and the vocabulary are the KJV's, the orthography is the writer's own.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

5:8.text: So when even was come, the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward, Call the labourers, and give them their hire, beginning from the last unto the first.

provenance.other: “lord of the vineyard” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Matthew 20:8, Mark 12:9, Luke 20:13 and Luke 20:15. All four are inside a parable — the labourers hired at the eleventh hour, and the husbandmen who kill the son. The Book of Mormon's own longest run against any of them stands at 5:71, where the 1830 text reads 'the Lord of the vineyard saith unto them' against Matthew 20:8's 'the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward' — seven consecutive words.
provenance.significance: The title by which God is named some fifty times in this chapter exists in the King James Bible only as the name of a character in two parables, and in both of them the vineyard is taken out of the hands of those who hold it. Recovering that context makes the allegory's ending predictable before it arrives: Matthew 20:8's lord pays 'beginning from the last unto the first', and Jacob 5:63 will graft 'beginning at the last, that they may be first'. The Book of Mormon has not merely borrowed a title; it has borrowed the parable the title belongs to and finished it differently.

5:8.note: 'And behold, saith the Lord of the vineyard, I take away many of these young and tender branches.' First appearance of the chapter's governing title. The 1830 text is also evidence here: it spells the verb 'sayeth' twenty-six times in this chapter and 'saith' only six, and the KJV form clusters exactly where the KJV phrase does — 5:8, 5:31 and 5:71, all three of them 'the Lord of the vineyard saith'. Where the borrowed formula is in play the borrowed spelling comes with it.

5:9.text: Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?

provenance.other: “why cumbereth it the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verb 'cumber' occurs in only one other place in the Authorized Version, Luke 10:40, where Martha is 'cumbered about much serving'. There is no other biblical warrant for the idea of a plant cumbering ground.
provenance.significance: Luke 13:6-9 is the one KJV parable in which an owner wants a fruitless tree destroyed, a servant asks for a stay, and the tree is given one more season of digging and dunging. Jacob 5 keeps every element and multiplies it: the complaint at 5:9 and 5:49, the servant's stay at 5:27 and 5:50, the digging and dunging at 5:47 and 5:76. The whole seventy-seven-verse shape of the allegory — a proprietor repeatedly talked out of felling — is Luke 13:6-9 held open.

5:9.note: 'These which I have plucked off, I will cast into the fire, and burn them, that they may not cumber the ground of my vineyard.' Cumbering the ground is Luke's idea and Luke's word, and the Book of Mormon uses it three times (5:9, 5:49, 5:66), always of what must be cleared out of the vineyard. Note that the KJV asks it as a question and the Book of Mormon states it as a purpose, which is the usual direction of this chapter's borrowing: Luke's parable poses the problem, Zenos's allegory acts on it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

5:18.text: Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.

provenance.other: No distinctive phrase is reproduced; the terms shared with Romans 11:18 are 'root' and 'branches', both common. What is not common is the proposition — that the root carries the grafted branch and not the reverse — which the Bible states only here.
provenance.significance: Paul warns the grafted wild branch not to boast against the natural ones, because 'thou bearest not the root, but the root thee'. Jacob 5:18 is that sentence turned into narrative fact: the wild branches bear tame fruit only 'because of the much strength of the root thereof'. Then the allegory does what Paul only threatens. At 5:37 the wild branches 'have overran the roots thereof', at 5:48 the servant diagnoses the ruin as branches overcoming the roots, and at 5:65-66 the remedy is to keep root and top equal in strength so that neither overpowers the other. The catalogue's claim at 1 Nephi 10:12 was that Romans 11 is this book's master allegory; this is the row where Romans 11 supplies not a phrase but a mechanism.

5:18.note: 'The branches of the wild tree hath taken hold of the moisture of the root thereof, that the root thereof hath brought forth much strength; and because of the much strength of the root thereof, the wild branches hath brought forth tame fruit.' There is no wording to count here, which is why kjvSpecific is left uncertain and the subtype is conceptual. The claim is that the chapter's whole physiology of root and branch, including the disaster at 5:37-48 and the balancing rule at 5:66, is an exposition of one sentence of Paul that has no other biblical statement.

5:22.text: For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?
5:22.whyNot: Two words, and common ones. 'Counsel me not' shares nothing distinctive with Romans 11:34 beyond the root 'counsel', and a master rebuking a servant for second-guessing him needs no source. The row rests entirely on position: the rebuke stands inside an allegory built out of Romans 11, at the point where the servant questions the Lord's choice of ground.

provenance.route: Romans 11:34 (quoting Isaiah 40:13) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “his counsellor” occurs in eight KJV verses, so nothing here is decided by rarity. Romans 11:34 quotes Isaiah 40:13, and mediation cannot be settled: tools/mediation-check.py finds no point where the two versions differ that the Book of Mormon's two words reproduce.
provenance.significance: Romans 11 ends by forbidding exactly the question the servant asks. Paul closes the olive-tree argument with 'who hath been his counsellor?', and Jacob 5's servant, having asked why the Lord planted in the poorest spot of ground, is told 'Counsel me not'. If the allegory is an expansion of Romans 11 — which 5:7 and 5:18 argue — then it has expanded the doxology too, and made the unanswerable question into a scene.

5:22.note: 'Counsel me not: I knew that it was a poor spot of ground.' Recorded at moderate as a positional echo rather than a verbal one. Compare Romans 9:20 for the same rebuke in a different figure. The interest is that this chapter's only moment of friction between servant and master falls where Romans 11's own argument runs out.

5:26.text: Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.

provenance.other: “beareth not fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “every branch in me” in exactly one, both John 15:2; “and they are burned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 15:6, whose 'men gather them, and cast them into the fire' is the source of this chapter's standing formula.
provenance.significance: John 15 is the one place in the KJV where the owner of the plant is the Father, the pruning is his own act, and the removed branches are gathered and burned — which is precisely the division of labour in Jacob 5, and precisely what Isaiah 5 and Luke 13 do not supply (Isaiah's owner destroys the whole vineyard; Luke's owner delegates to a hired dresser). 1 Nephi 15:15 had already put John's vine beside Paul's olive tree in a single sentence; here the two are fused for seventy-seven verses, and the seam shows only in the vocabulary.

5:26.note: 'Pluck off the branches that have not brought forth good fruit, and cast them into the fire.' Both halves are KJV singletons from the same passage: John 15:2's branch that beareth not fruit and is taken away, John 15:6's branches cast into the fire and burned. The Book of Mormon's formula 'cast them into the fire' recurs at 5:7, 5:9, 5:42, 5:49, 5:58 and 5:66, and John 15:6 is one of only two KJV verses to contain it. Matthew 7:19 supplies the other governing form, 'bringeth not forth good fruit … hewn down, and cast into the fire', which is catalogued separately at 5:42.

5:27.text: And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down.

provenance.other: “let it alone this year” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 13:8, and it is the only reprieve granted to a tree anywhere in the Bible. The whole conditional shape — one more term of cultivation, then the axe if nothing comes — exists only at Luke 13:8-9.
provenance.significance: The servant's intercession is the structural engine of Jacob 5, and it is Luke's invention. Three times an owner resolves to destroy and three times a servant asks for delay (5:27, 5:50, and by implication 5:34), and each time the delay is granted on Luke's terms: more labour now, judgment deferred. Metalepsis in the strict sense — the point of the borrowing lies in what Luke 13:9 says next and Jacob 5 does not, that if the tree still fails 'then after that thou shalt cut it down', which is what 5:42 and 5:49 finally propose.

5:27.note: 'Let us prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it a little longer, that perhaps it may bring forth good fruit unto thee.' The servant's speech reproduces the dresser's: cultivation named in the same order, a probationary period, and a conditional hope of fruit. At 5:50 it shortens to 'Spare it a little longer', and the Lord grants it in the same words at 5:51. No clause is reproduced verbatim, but the scene is Luke's scene and its vocabulary was already shown to be Luke's at 5:4.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

5:32.text: And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.

provenance.other: “profiteth me nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:3.
provenance.significance: The verdict on the vineyard is delivered in the phrase Paul reserves for works done without charity. Both sentences describe an expenditure of labour that yields a return the speaker cannot use — 'notwithstanding all our labor' answers 'though I bestow all my goods' — and in both the failure is not of quantity but of kind.

5:32.note: 'It profiteth me nothing, notwithstanding all our labor.' A four-word KJV singleton in a sentence about fruitless effort, which is 1 Corinthians 13:3's subject. Held at moderate: the phrase is ordinary English as well as Pauline English, and the sense is not distinctively Paul's. It is recorded because the count is absolute and the surrounding clause about labour spent for nothing sharpens it.

5:35.text: Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.

provenance.other: “availeth me nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The construction it belongs to — a verb of profit, 'me nothing', and a 'so long as' clause naming the single thing that spoils an otherwise complete satisfaction — occurs nowhere else in the Authorized Version.
provenance.significance: Haman has just recited his honours and finds them worthless while one man sits unbowed at the gate; the Lord of the vineyard has just been told his roots are alive and finds them worthless while the tree bears evil fruit. The syntax carries the psychology: a grievance that cannot be answered by any addition, only by the removal of the one thing. It is the least likely source in the chapter and the most exactly matched sentence-shape in it.

5:35.note: 'The tree profiteth me nothing; and the roots thereof profiteth me nothing, so long as it shall bring forth evil fruit.' The n-gram stream proposed Esther 5:13 here on the runs 'me nothing so long' and 'nothing so long as', and on reading it holds: the KJV has exactly one sentence of this shape. The 1830 reading matters. The first edition writes 'the roots thereof profiteth me nothing', with Esther's singular verb; the 1920 edition changed the second verb to 'profit' and broke the parallel, so the borrowing is plainer in the running text than in the modern one.

5:41.text: What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes?

provenance.other: “what could have been done more” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon puts the question in the first person and the active voice — 'What could I have done more for my vineyard?' — which is the only substantive change; every content word is Isaiah's, in Isaiah's order.
provenance.significance: The sentence is asked three times in this chapter (5:41, 5:47, 5:49), and each time it is asked it does more of Isaiah's work. At 5:41 it is the lament; at 5:47 it is answered item by item, which is what Isaiah 5:4 only implies ('that I have not done in it'); at 5:49 it justifies the sentence of destruction, which is Isaiah 5:5-6. And Isaiah 5:7 supplies the identification the allegory opened with at 5:3: 'the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel'. Isaiah asks the question and moves immediately to destruction; Zenos asks it and then refuses to act on it for another thirty verses. That refusal is the whole argument of Jacob 5, and it is legible only against Isaiah 5.

5:41.note: 'And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard wept, and sayeth unto the servant, What could I have done more for my vineyard?' A complete clause reproduced from a KJV singleton, with the voice changed from passive to first-person active. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his catalogued quotations; it is entered as a quotation on the strength of the absolute rarity and of the surrounding structure, which is Isaiah 5:1-7 in sequence. Isaiah's owner does not weep, and the tear is the allegory's addition.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

5:42.text: Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: “hewn down” occurs in five KJV verses and “cast into the fire” in five; the three that contain both are Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9, and all three say it of a tree that brings forth no good fruit. “good for nothing” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 13:10 and Matthew 5:13.
provenance.significance: The sentence Jacob 5 passes on the vineyard is the Baptist's sentence, and Matthew 7:19 is the shortest form of it. What the borrowing brings with it is the axe already laid to the root (Matthew 3:10, Luke 3:9), which is why the chapter's crisis is a crisis about roots. Note also that 'good for nothing, save it be to be hewn down' fuses Matthew 5:13's verdict on savourless salt with the Baptist's verdict on fruitless trees — two judgment sayings from the same Gospel, welded at the seam.

5:42.note: 'All the trees of my vineyard are good for nothing, save it be to be hewn down and cast into the fire.' The n-gram stream ranks this run at 5:42, 5:46 and 5:66, and it is a genuine seven-word agreement with a formula the KJV states three times. Adjudicated here at first full use; the later occurrences are the chapter reusing its own borrowed formula.

5:43.text: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.

provenance.other: “fruitful hill” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “gathered out the stones” in exactly one and “choicest vine” in exactly one, all of them Isaiah 5:1-2.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's owner does three things before planting: he takes very good ground, clears what is in it, and puts in the choicest stock. Jacob 5:43-44 does the same three in the same order — a spot 'choice unto me, above all other parts of the land', then 'I also cut down that which cumbered this spot of ground, that I might plant this tree in the stead thereof'. And the outcome is Isaiah's outcome, stated in Isaiah's antithesis: part brought forth good fruit and part wild fruit, where Isaiah looked for grapes and got wild grapes. This is the passage of the chapter that is closest to being a retelling rather than an allusion.

5:43.note: 'This last, whose branch hath withered away, I did plant in a good spot of ground; yea, even that which was choice unto me, above all other parts of the land of my vineyard.' No phrase is reproduced, but the sequence of preparation is Isaiah 5:2's and the disappointment is Isaiah 5:2's, and the chapter has already quoted Isaiah 5:4 two verses earlier. Held at moderate because the three rarity counts belong to words the Book of Mormon does not use — it says 'choice' for 'choicest', 'cut down that which cumbered' for 'gathered out the stones'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

5:47.text: But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:2 → Romans 10:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “spread out my hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezra 9:5 and Isaiah 65:2. Romans 10:21 quotes Isaiah 65:2 and changes its verb: the Old Testament has 'I have spread out my hands all the day', the New Testament has 'All day long I have stretched forth my hands'. tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive divergence and the Book of Mormon is on the New Testament side of it.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 65:2, if 'stretched forth' is treated as a natural English variation rather than a borrowing. The word order tells against that: 'all the day long' keeps Isaiah's 'all the day' and adds Paul's 'long', so the clause is a hybrid, and a hybrid presupposes both texts.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's mediation test and it resolves cleanly. Where the KJV Old Testament and the KJV New Testament word the same sentence differently, Jacob 5:47 has the New Testament's word — 'stretched forth', not 'spread out' — which places it with the sixteen OT-via-NT rows that were the 1 Nephi pilot's principal result. What comes with Romans 10:21 is its addressee: Paul's 'But to Israel he saith' is the header of the quotation, and Jacob 5 is Zenos speaking to the house of Israel. Isaiah 65:2 has the same sense but not the same audience marked in the verse.

5:47.note: 'I have stretched forth mine hand almost all the day long; and the end draweth nigh.' The verse is a knot of three sources: Isaiah 5:4's question opens it ('what could I have done more in my vineyard?'), Luke 13:8's verbs fill its middle ('I have digged it … I have dunged it'), and its climax is Romans 10:21. The mediation is decided by one word. Isaiah 65:2 reads 'spread out', Romans 10:21 reads 'stretched forth', and the Book of Mormon reads 'stretched forth'. The one change the Book of Mormon makes is its own: it inserts 'almost', which neither source has, and which converts a complaint of unlimited patience into a patience that is running out — the point the next clause makes explicit.

5:48.text: And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.

provenance.other: “loftiness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 2:17 and Jeremiah 48:29, and in both it means pride, not height, and in both it is about to be brought down.
provenance.significance: The servant's diagnosis of the vineyard uses a word the Authorized Version reserves for the arrogance that the day of the Lord humbles. That is a moral term inserted into what is otherwise a purely horticultural explanation — the branches grew faster than the roots could bear — and it is the only place in seventy-seven verses where the allegory names the failure as a sin rather than as a botanical accident.

5:48.note: 'Is it not the loftiness of thy vineyard? Hath not the branches thereof overcame the roots, which are good?' The 1830 reading is 'overcame' where 1920 reads 'overcome'. Held at moderate: one word, and the Book of Mormon's syntax is its own. The case is that the word is rare, that both its KJV occurrences carry the same moral charge, and that it does work here no other word in the sentence does. Compare Romans 11:18 at 5:18 — Paul forbids the grafted branch to boast against the root, and this is that boast succeeding.

5:63.text: So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.

provenance.other: “the last shall be first” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 19:30 and Matthew 20:16, and both belong to the same discourse. “beginning from the last” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:8, and “labourers into his vineyard” in exactly one, Matthew 20:1.
provenance.significance: This is where the borrowing catalogued at 5:8 pays out. The title 'Lord of the vineyard' came from Matthew 20:8; Matthew 20:8's own sentence continues 'beginning from the last unto the first', and Matthew 20:16 draws the moral 'the last shall be first, and the first last'. Jacob 5:63 has both halves — 'begin at the last, that they may be first, and that the first may be last' — applied not to wages but to grafting order. Recover the parable and the reading changes: in Matthew the reversal is a scandal to the labourers hired first, and here it is simply the method by which the vineyard is saved. The allegory has taken Matthew's most contested saying and made it a horticultural instruction.

5:63.note: 'Graft in the branches: begin at the last, that they may be first, and that the first may be last, and dig about the trees, both old and young, the first and the last, and the last and the first.' The saying is diffused across four KJV verses (Matthew 19:30, 20:16, Mark 10:31, Luke 13:30) and would be weak evidence alone; what makes the case is that this chapter has already taken its name for God from the one parable in which the saying is worked out with labourers, a vineyard, and a payment order that literally begins from the last. The n-gram stream proposed Revelation 1:11 here on 'the first and the last', which is the wrong source — see the exclusion register.

5:65.text: But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.

provenance.other: “lest while ye gather” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “root up also the wheat” in exactly one, both Matthew 13:29. No word of either is reproduced, which is why kjvSpecific is left uncertain; what is reproduced is the argument, which the Bible makes only here.
provenance.significance: Matthew 13:29 is the one place in scripture where evil is left standing on purpose, and for a stated reason: uprooting it now would take the good with it. Jacob 5:65 gives that reason a mechanism — clear the bad away too fast and the roots will overpower the graft — and 5:66 gives it a rule, that the root and the top be kept equal in strength. Then 5:77 ends the allegory where Matthew 13:30 ends the parable, with a final separation of good from bad at the harvest. The Book of Mormon has taken the parable of the tares and rewritten it as horticulture.

5:65.note: 'Ye shall not clear away the bad thereof, all at once, lest the roots thereof should be too strong for the graft, and the graft thereof shall perish.' The verbal contact is one word, 'lest'. The case for the link is the reasoning: a delayed purge, justified by the risk to the good, which is Matthew 13:29's proposition and no other verse's. Recorded at high because that proposition is distinctive and because the chapter closes on Matthew 13's harvest imagery at 5:77.

5:68.text: Say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine hand.

provenance.other: “they shall be one” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 2:24 and Ezekiel 37:19. Genesis is about marriage; Ezekiel is about two separated portions of Israel joined in the Lord's hand, which is the subject of this verse. “one fold” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:16, already catalogued at 1 Nephi 15:15.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 37's two sticks — Joseph's and Judah's — made one in the Lord's hand is the Book of Mormon's own charter text for what it takes itself to be, and Jacob 5 ends by performing it: branches scattered to the nethermost parts are grafted back into the mother tree until 'they shall be one' and, at 5:74, 'they became like unto one body'. The allegory's addition to Romans 11 was always the hidden branches; Ezekiel is where the hidden branch has a name.

5:68.note: 'Thus will I bring them together again, that they shall bring forth the natural fruit: and they shall be one.' Three common words, and the count is only two — but the two are Genesis's marriage and Ezekiel's reunification, and only one of those is about Israel divided and restored. Held at moderate on that basis. The 'one body' of 5:74 pulls in the Pauline figure as well, which is why the composite names John 10:16's fold rather than settling on a single image: the chapter is assembling every KJV figure for incorporation, exactly as 1 Nephi 15:15 does in one sentence.

5:70.text: Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;

provenance.other: “the labourers are few” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 9:37 and Luke 10:2, and both are the same saying. “labourers into his vineyard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:1.
provenance.significance: The sentence in Matthew is a call for more workers because the ones available cannot cover the harvest, and the sentence in Jacob 5 is the same shortage answered the same way: the servant is sent for others and comes back with few, and the Lord of the vineyard then labours alongside them (5:72). The one thing the Book of Mormon adds is the master in the field, which neither Matthew 9 nor Matthew 20 has.

5:70.note: 'The servant went and did as the Lord had commanded him, and brought other servants; and they were few.' The clause is not reproduced — 'they were few' against 'the labourers are few' — but the situation is the KJV's, and 5:71's 'Go to, and labor in the vineyard' returns to the hiring of Matthew 20:1. Recorded at moderate; the shortage of labourers is a natural thing to say, and the count of two is what keeps it in the catalogue.

5:75.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

provenance.other: “thou good and faithful servant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:21, and “the joy of thy lord” in exactly two, Matthew 25:21 and 25:23, which are the same commendation spoken twice.
provenance.significance: The allegory ends with the scene the KJV keeps for the end of the world: a lord returning, finding his servants diligent, and admitting them to his own joy. But the Book of Mormon changes the preposition and the direction. Matthew's servant is told to 'enter thou into the joy of thy lord'; Zenos's servants are told 'ye shall have joy with me' — joy shared in the field rather than joy entered as a reward, which is consistent with 5:72, where the Lord of the vineyard has been labouring beside them. The commendation formula is Matthew's; the fellowship in it is not.

5:75.note: 'Blessed art thou. For because that ye have been diligent in laboring with me in my vineyard, and have kept my commandments … ye shall have joy with me, because of the fruit of my vineyard.' A commendation for diligence over a long stewardship, ending in the lord's joy — Matthew 25:21 without the reproduced clause. The 1830 text reads 'he calleth up his servants and sayeth unto them' and keeps the singular 'blessed art thou' inside a plural address, a rough seam the later editions did not smooth.

5:77.text: Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.

provenance.other: “gathered the good” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “cast the bad away” occurs in exactly one, both Matthew 13:48. The pairing of 'the good' and 'the bad' as the two halves of a final sorting exists nowhere else in the Authorized Version.
provenance.significance: The last verse of the allegory is Matthew 13's parable chapter compressed. The dragnet supplies the sorting — the good gathered and kept, the bad cast away; the tares supply the burning at the end of the age, 'as therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world' (13:40); and 13:49's 'So shall it be at the end of the world' supplies the timetable that Zenos states as 'then cometh the season and the end'. Read back into the chapter, this is what makes 5:65's delayed purge intelligible: the allegory has been running Matthew 13 from the tares to the dragnet, and it ends where Matthew ends.

5:77.note: 'Then will I cause the good and the bad to be gathered; and the good will I preserve unto myself; and the bad will I cast away into its own place. And then cometh the season and the end; and my vineyard will I cause to be burned with fire.' Two KJV singletons split across one sentence, in Matthew's order, with 'preserve' substituted for 'gathered … into vessels' — the chapter's own word, used thirteen times before this. The n-gram stream proposed Jeremiah 38:23 here for 'to be burned with fire', which is the wrong source; see the exclusion register.
